idiom_name: collection-owned traversal message taking an element action (do: / each / forEach) with a cursor or callback as the carrier
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the collection exposes one operation that walks its elements itself and applies a caller-supplied action to each, so clients never compute indices or hold a cursor. Two carriers exist: a callback/block (the action is passed in; used by Smalltalk do:, Ruby each, Kotlin/Swift forEach) and a cursor object the collection creates (next/isDone; used by Iterator, IEnumerator, __next__). The transforming siblings - collect/select/reject/inject (map/filter/fold) - are the same message returning a derived value instead of nothing. Keep the traversal implementation (order, laziness, removal rules) inside the collection, reuse one implementation for all call sites, and provide a dedicated message for the cases a callback cannot express: early exit (detect/find) and removal during the walk.
code_sketch:
for each element of collection:
    action(element)                     # collection decides how it walks
# siblings returning values:
#   map(action), filter(predicate), fold(initial, combine)
# early exit / removal need their own messages, not a flag inside action
pitfalls: Letting the action mutate the collection recreates the traversal hazard the pattern hides; the walk must collect changes and apply them afterwards.
Sharing one traversal implementation with a leaked index or cursor (a public counter) re-exposes the state the pattern was meant to encapsulate.
A callback-only protocol with no early-exit message forces a flag variable, which is an index loop in disguise.

Wrong move: adding or removing elements inside the action -> the walk throws (Java's ConcurrentModificationException), silently skips elements (Python lists, JavaScript forEach) or is undefined behaviour (C++ iterators) -> instead record what must change during the walk and apply it afterwards, or use the collection's dedicated removal message (removeIf, retainAll, Rust retain/drain, g_hash_table_foreach_remove).

Wrong move: awaiting an async action inside a synchronous forEach -> every callback starts an unawaited task, elements run concurrently instead of in sequence, and rejections surface as unhandled promise errors -> instead use the language's async iteration form (for await...of, Kotlin Flow, async stream/iterator protocols), which drives the walk one element at a time.

Wrong move: building a lazy pipeline - LINQ query, Java stream, Rust adapter chain - and never consuming it -> nothing happens: no elements visited, no side effects run, and the omission fails silently -> instead treat consumption as part of the call contract: end every chain with a terminal consumer (forEach/for_each, collect, count) or materialise eagerly when the walk is performed for its effects.
